nameStory: Dwarf mallow earned its name from its low-growing habit, rarely reaching more than two feet tall, making it the shortest member of the mallow family you're likely to encounter. The 'mallow' part comes from the Old English 'malwe,' referring to the soft, mucilaginous texture of the leaves when crushed. It's also called 'cheeseplant' because its round, flat seed pods look remarkably like tiny wheels of cheese!
description: Dwarf mallow is a sprawling annual plant that hugs the ground, growing in a circular mat pattern rather than standing upright. It typically reaches only 6-24 inches tall but can spread much wider, with round, wrinkled leaves and tiny pale pink or white flowers that appear almost too small for the robust plant. The whole plant has a soft, velvety feel and produces distinctive round, flat seed pods that look like miniature cheese wheels. Originally from Europe and Asia, it's now a common sight throughout New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Round to kidney-shaped leaves with shallow lobes radiating from the center like fingers on a hand, feeling soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch with prominent veins creating a wrinkled texture

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale pink or white flowers with five petals that are often barely noticeable, tucked close to where the leaf stems meet the main stem

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive round, flat seed pods that break apart like orange segments, earning the nickname 'cheeses' - they're green when young, turning brown and papery when mature

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in a prostrate, sprawling pattern forming circular mats on the ground rather than growing upright, with stems radiating outward from the center

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant feels soft and velvety due to fine hairs covering leaves and stems, and crushed leaves release a slightly mucilaginous (slimy) sap

habitat: Dwarf mallow thrives in disturbed soils and can be found in lawns, garden beds, sidewalk cracks, vacant lots, and along roadsides throughout New England. It prefers sunny locations with rich, moist soil but is remarkably adaptable to poor conditions. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy species like dandelions and plantains in urban and suburban settings.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with the characteristic round, lobed leaves appearing soft and bright green. Early flowers may begin appearing in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing and flowering season, with plants forming full circular mats and producing their tiny flowers continuously. This is the best time to spot the distinctive cheese-wheel seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue growing and flowering until frost, with mature seed pods turning brown and splitting open to release seeds. Late-season plants may be quite large and sprawling.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving no above-ground trace, but seeds remain in the soil ready to germinate the following spring.

funFact: The seeds of dwarf mallow are incredibly nutritious, containing 21% protein and 15% fat - making them more protein-rich than many nuts, and they taste like tiny sunflower seeds when eaten raw!
confusionNotes: Dwarf mallow is most easily confused with other low-growing weeds, but its distinctive round, lobed leaves with the wrinkled, velvety texture are unique. Remember: if the leaves look like tiny hands with stubby fingers and feel like velvet, you've found your mallow!
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'neglecta' fool you - this plant is far from neglected! It's one of the most widespread edible weeds in the world, and despite being called 'common mallow' in some places, it's actually the dwarf species. The entire plant is edible and has been used as food and medicine for thousands of years.
compareHints: Unlike its cousin musk mallow which grows upright with deeply divided leaves, dwarf mallow stays low and sprawling with round, shallowly-lobed leaves. Common mallow is much taller and more upright, while dwarf mallow's prostrate growth habit and smaller flowers make it easy to distinguish. The 'cheese wheel' seed pods are shared among mallows, but dwarf mallow's ground-hugging growth is distinctive in the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's mallows, musk mallow stands out with its deeply-cut, narrow leaf segments - quite different from the broad, rounded leaves of common mallow or the small, kidney-shaped leaves of dwarf mallow.

Among its mallow relatives, greater musk-mallow stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - they're cut almost to the midrib unlike the merely lobed leaves of common mallow or the heart-shaped leaves of dwarf mallow.
Common mallow stands out from other New England mallows by being the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most intensely colored flowers.
Unlike the perennial musk mallow with its deeply divided leaves and smaller flowers, Royal Mallow is an annual with simpler heart-shaped leaves and much larger blooms.
Among New England's mallows, cheeseweed mallow is distinguished by having the smallest flowers and the smoothest seed pods.
Eastern Tree-mallow stands out from other mallows in New England primarily by its exceptional height - it can reach 6 feet compared to the 1-3 feet typical of Musk Mallow or Common Mallow.
